entry.title: David
entry.creator: Michelangelo Buonarroti
entry.body:
In the biblical story, David is a young shepherd who offers to fight Goliath, the armed champion frightening Israel’s soldiers. He rejects the king’s armor and confronts him with a sling and a stone, trusting in God. His victory makes him a model of strength that does not depend on size or military equipment.

Michelangelo shows David before the fight. The sling lies over his shoulder, his brow is drawn, and his head turns toward an opponent we cannot see. There is no defeated giant at his feet. The still body and concentrated gaze direct attention to his readiness for the encounter. His muscular, nude figure recalls ancient heroic sculpture, while the small weapon keeps the biblical story recognizable.

The statue’s enormous scale had a practical origin. Commissioned in 1501, it was intended for a high buttress on Florence’s cathedral, where people would see it from far below. In 1504, a committee chose a different location: beside the entrance to the city’s government palace.

Florence already used David as a symbol of its capacity to resist stronger opponents. At the palace, the religious hero became a public emblem of the republic’s independence. The change of location gave his watchful stance a political role, placing a defender outside the building where the city was governed.

changes: Introduces the biblical unequal fight and religious trust before interpreting the figure.
Removes the claim that the sculpture depicts an exact moment of deciding what to do.
Explains the cathedral’s high intended placement and the later civic relocation.

entry.meaningBrief: The biblical underdog becomes an alert, monumental defender before battle. Cathedral viewing conditions explain the scale, and relocation beside the government palace gives the inherited religious subject a specific republican role. The prose avoids assigning an unobservable decision to David.
quotationNotes: No direct quotations. Biblical narrative paraphrased; no translation quoted.

selectedOption.fidelityNotes: Broad face identity, pose, gaze and hand position remain recognizable. Fine marble speckling and hair texture are regenerated, so this is not pixel-preserving or a conservation reference. Compare the source before approving.
selectedOption.generationPrompt: Precise sculpture photograph edit. Image 1 is an authentic photograph of Michelangelo's original David in the Accademia, Florence. Image 2 provides BACKGROUND STYLE ONLY. Keep image 1's exact photographed head, neck, sling and visible shoulder/hand. Keep the same three-quarter camera view, expression, eye direction, hair carving, marble color, weathering, face proportions and lighting. Replace the architectural background only with near-black at the top, grading very subtly to charcoal toward the bottom like image 2. Compose a close head-and-shoulder portrait in a 4:5 frame; add approximately 15% black headroom by extending BACKGROUND ONLY, no new sculpture. Keep existing foreground intact and crop only at the lower edge if needed. Do not invent a new camera elevation, rotate or reshape the head, beautify, repair damage, sharpen by adding texture, invent hidden surfaces or borrow features from Caracalla. No text or watermark.
